title: Two Branches of the Herrin Family Reunite
summary: How two branches of a Georgia family, descended from Levi Herrin and Charity Sears, came together through the marriage of William Levi Herrin and Laura Etta Palmer in April 1916.
author: Family Archive Research

sections.heading: A Family Takes Root in Georgia
sections.text: In the middle of the nineteenth century, southeastern Georgia was home to a growing family whose descendants would eventually follow two different paths before coming together again generations later. At the center of this story were Levi Herrin, born around 1804, and his wife, Charity Sears. By 1850, Levi and Charity were living in Ware County, Georgia, where the federal census recorded a large household that included William Herring, age 19, and Charlotte Herring, age 13. Their surname appeared as Herring in the census, one of the spelling variations found in historical records of the family. William and Charlotte would become central figures in two branches of the Herrin family. William's branch would eventually lead to his grandson, William Levi Herrin. Charlotte's branch would lead to her granddaughter, Laura Etta Palmer. Generations later, those two descendants would marry, bringing the family lines together again.

sections.heading: William M. Herrin and Mary Hargraves
sections.text: On January 3, 1853, William M. Herrin married Mary Hargraves in Ware County, Georgia. Mary was the daughter of Thomas Hopewell Hargraves and Nancy Beverly. Like William, she had been living in Ware County when the 1850 federal census was taken. Interestingly, their families appeared just twelve household numbers apart in that census. Although this does not establish how close their homes were, it places both families in the same census enumeration area several years before their marriage. On May 22, 1854, their son Thomas Levi Herrin was born. The family continued to grow, and by 1870 the census recorded William and Mary living in Ware County with Thomas and several other children. Thomas later married Nancy T. Jewell. Their son, William Levi Herrin, was born on May 4, 1892, in Homerville, Georgia. Through William Levi, the first branch of our story was approaching the generation in which the family lines would meet again.

sections.heading: Charlotte Herrin and the Williams Family
sections.text: While William M. Herrin was establishing his family with Mary Hargraves, another branch of the Herrin family was beginning to take shape. William's younger sister, Charlotte Herrin, was born around 1837 in Georgia. She appears in the 1850 federal census living in the household of Levi and Charity Herrin in Ware County. Around 1854, Charlotte married Hezekiah Ponder Williams in Clinch County, Georgia. Hezekiah, born in 1828, was the son of John Williams Sr. and Nancy Smith. On April 29, 1855, their daughter Laura Williams was born. Laura later married Henry Palmer, and on June 25, 1898, their daughter Laura Etta was born in Pearson, Georgia. Laura Etta's name appears in historical records as Lauretta, Laura, Laura E and Laura Etta. Through her grandmother Charlotte, Laura Etta shared ancestry with William Levi Herrin, the grandson of Charlotte's brother, William M. Herrin.

sections.heading: Two Branches Reunited
sections.text: In April 1916, in Clinch County, Georgia, William Levi Herrin and Laura Etta Palmer were married. Their marriage represented more than the beginning of a new family. It brought together two branches of the Herrin family that had descended from the same ancestors several generations earlier. William Levi traced his ancestry through Thomas Levi Herrin and William M. Herrin to Levi Herrin and Charity Sears. Laura Etta traced her ancestry through Laura Williams and Charlotte Herrin to the same couple. According to the reconstructed family lineage, William Levi and Laura Etta were third cousins. Whether they knew about their shared ancestry when they married is unknown. Their descendants would carry forward the history of both branches, including their daughter Ollie Mae Herrin, born September 6, 1917, in Homerville, Georgia. Their story reminds us that family history is more than a collection of names and dates. It is the story of generations whose lives intersect in ways they may never have fully understood.

sections.heading: Sources and Research Notes
sections.text: The 1850 United States census for Ware County, Georgia, records William and Charlotte Herring in the household of Levi and Charity Herring. The 1870 census records William Herring, Mary Herring, and Thomas L. Herring in the same household. The marriage of William M. Herrin and Mary Hargraves on January 3, 1853, and the marriage of William Levi Herrin and Laura Etta Palmer in April 1916 are dates provided through family research. An original marriage document for the 1916 marriage has not yet been obtained. Some parent-child relationships in the reconstructed lineage require additional independent documentation.

title: Family Ties in the 26th Georgia Infantry — Draft - Research in Progress
summary: An ongoing account of relatives connected to the 26th Georgia Infantry, including the Herrin and Williams families, and the records documenting their individual experiences.
author: Art Singletary

sections.heading: Family Connections
sections.text: Several members of our extended family appear in records of the 26th Georgia Infantry, a Confederate regiment organized at Brunswick, Georgia, in 1861. Its companies drew recruits from southeastern Georgia, including Ware County, where several branches of our family lived. This developing story brings together their individual records and family connections.

sections.heading: William M. Herrin
sections.text: William M. Herrin, my third great-grandfather, served as a Private in Company K. His military record cover identifies his unit and rank, and his wife Mary Hargraves Herrin's later Confederate widow's pension file provides additional evidence of that service. His enlistment and discharge dates, assignments, and individual wartime experiences remain under review.

sections.heading: Three Williams Brothers in Company K
sections.text: A family-history article by Frances Vickers Wilkes, titled "John Williams Family of Red Bluff" and published in The Douglas Enterprise on January 5, 1994, page 8-C, identifies three sons of my fourth great-grandfather John Williams and his wife Nancy Smith as serving together in Company K, 26th Georgia Infantry. They were Hezekiah Ponder Williams, Jackson S. "Tobe" Williams, and William M. Williams. These brothers therefore shared a company with William M. Herrin, according to the records collected so far, although their periods of overlapping service have not yet been established.

sections.heading: Hezekiah Ponder Williams
sections.text: Hezekiah Ponder Williams, my third great-grandfather, married Charlotte Herrin, a sister of William M. Herrin. The 1994 family-history article reports that Ponder was commissioned an ensign in the local Georgia militia on July 6, 1861, and later enlisted as a Private in Company K, 26th Georgia Infantry, on April 20, 1862. It states that a company roll dated November 5, 1864, listed him as sick and absent. According to the article, he was permitted to return home to the Red Bluff community and was unable to rejoin his command. It records his parole at Thomasville on May 21, 1865. These details will be compared with his military records.

sections.heading: Jackson S. "Tobe" Williams
sections.text: Jackson S. Williams, known as Tobe, was another son of John Williams and Nancy Smith. The 1994 article reports that he enlisted at Waresboro in Company K, 26th Georgia Infantry, on May 10, 1862, following his brothers Ponder and William M. It states that he served three years. His individual service records will be reviewed to establish further details.

sections.heading: William M. Williams
sections.text: William M. Williams, a son of John Williams and Nancy Smith and my third great-granduncle, is identified in the 1994 article as a member of Company K, 26th Georgia Infantry. The article reports that he was killed at Spotsylvania, Virginia, on May 12, 1864. His military records will be examined to corroborate this account. The article prints his birth year as 1943, an evident chronological error; his correct birth year requires separate verification.

sections.heading: Richmond Herrin
sections.text: Richmond Herrin, my third great-granduncle, appears in a published roster under the spelling Richmond Herren, with Herrin noted as an alternate spelling. The supplied roster extract identifies him as a Ware County resident who enlisted as a Private in Company L, 26th Georgia Infantry, on May 23, 1861. It records his death on December 30, 1862, at Chimborazo Hospital in Richmond, Virginia. The extract does not state a cause of death.

sections.heading: Manning Smith
sections.text: Manning Smith, my fourth great-granduncle, is listed in a supplied extract from the Roster of Confederate Soldiers of Georgia 1861–1865 as a Private in Company H, 26th Georgia Infantry. His enlistment and muster date are recorded as February 25, 1862. His subsequent service and wartime outcome remain to be documented.

sections.heading: Additional Relatives Under Review
sections.text: Additional family connections under review include G. B. Blanton, believed to be Greenberry Blanton, the first husband of my third great-grandmother Sarah Wadsworth; Ephraim McClendon, the husband of my third great-aunt; and John Williams Jr., my third great-granduncle. Their soldier-list entries require further comparison with family and military records to confirm identities, companies, and individual service histories. The 1994 article's statement about three Williams brothers serving together names Hezekiah, Jackson, and William M.; it does not establish John Jr.'s service.

sections.heading: Sources and Research Notes
sections.text: Sources collected for this developing story include William Herrin's military service record cover; Mary Herrin's Confederate widow's pension file; supplied roster extracts for Richmond Herren and Manning Smith from the Roster of Confederate Soldiers of Georgia 1861–1865; and Frances Vickers Wilkes's article "John Williams Family of Red Bluff," published in The Douglas Enterprise on January 5, 1994, page 8-C. The newspaper article is a retrospective family history, and its military details require comparison with individual service records. It gives conflicting birth years of 1828 and 1829 for Hezekiah Ponder Williams and prints an impossible birth year of 1943 for William M. Williams. The regiment's history provides context but does not establish that every relative participated in every campaign or battle.

sections.heading: Continuing the Research
sections.text: This is a draft and an ongoing research story. Additional military records, pension applications, census records, family accounts, and other documents will help establish each man's experiences and the effects of the war on his family. Profile links and source citations will be expanded as records are reviewed.

title: A Fatal Encounter at Glenmore: Hiram Jackson Herrin, 1928 — Draft - Research in Progress
summary: An account of Hiram Jackson Herrin's death in an exchange of gunfire near his Glenmore home on October 14, 1928, based on contemporary newspaper reports, his death certificate, and family records.
author: Art Singletary

sections.heading: A Fatal Encounter
sections.text: On Sunday, October 14, 1928, Hiram Jackson Herrin died in an exchange of gunfire near his home at Glenmore in Ware County, Georgia. He was 58 years old. The following day, The Macon Telegraph reported the incident under the headline "Death Climaxes Duel With Guns." Its account described a confrontation between Herrin, a local farmer and businessman, and F. W. Ivey, a turpentine operator, on the public highway in front of Herrin's home.

sections.heading: The Newspaper Account
sections.text: According to The Macon Telegraph, officers reported that each man had fired one shot. Herrin died at the scene, while Ivey was taken to a hospital in Waycross with serious injuries. Although the newspaper described Ivey's condition as critical and predicted that he would not recover, the records collected so far do not establish his eventual fate.

sections.heading: What Led to the Shooting?
sections.text: The newspaper reported that the men had been at odds over business matters. It also acknowledged that the immediate circumstances were unknown and that the two men were alone when the shooting occurred. Although the headlines called the encounter a duel, the available reports do not establish that it was formally arranged. Who initiated the confrontation, what was said, and the sequence of the shots remain unknown.

sections.heading: The Man Behind the Headline
sections.text: Hiram was a son of William M. Herrin and Mary Hargraves. His gravestone records his birth as March 30, 1870, and his death certificate identifies his birthplace as Ware County, Georgia. On February 5, 1895, he married Nellie Ellington, later identified as Nellie Virginia Ellington Herrin. Their Ware County marriage record names him as H. J. Herring, reflecting a surname variation found in family records. By the time of his death, Hiram was living in Glenmore and working as a farmer. The newspaper also described him as a businessman.

sections.heading: Connecting the Records
sections.text: Both supplied newspaper clippings identify the deceased as H. D. Herrin, while his death certificate names him as Hiram Jackson Herrin and his gravestone reads Hiram J. Herrin. Their matching death date, location, and circumstances strongly support the identification despite the conflicting initials. His death certificate records a fatal gunshot injury and gives his age as 58 years, 6 months, and 14 days. That stated age differs slightly from the age calculated from the March 30, 1870 birth date on his gravestone.

sections.heading: Burial and Family Remembrance
sections.text: Hiram's death certificate records burial on October 15, 1928, at a place written as Indian Mount. His burial has been identified as Indian Mound Baptist Church Cemetery in Millwood, Ware County, Georgia. He rests in the Herrin Family Plot beside his wife, Nellie Virginia Ellington Herrin, whose gravestone records February 17, 1874 – September 30, 1960.

sections.heading: Questions for Further Research
sections.text: This account remains a work in progress. Further newspaper coverage, an inquest, or court records may help explain the business disagreement, clarify the circumstances of the shooting, and establish what happened to F. W. Ivey. Additional research may also explain why the newspapers used the initials H. D. rather than H. J. Until further evidence is found, the newspaper's claims are attributed to its reporting rather than presented as independently established facts.

sections.heading: Sources and Research Notes
sections.text: Sources include Hiram Jackson Herrin's Georgia death certificate, state file number 28071; the Ware County marriage record for H. J. Herring and Nellie Ellington, page 280; the photograph of Hiram and Nellie's graves; and the supplied newspaper clippings. The longer clipping is identified by its supplied filename as The Macon Telegraph, October 15, 1928. The shorter Associated Press clipping has a Waycross dateline of October 14, but its newspaper title and publication date have not yet been established.

title: Eller Juanita Tuten and Trixy: Together Even in Death
summary: The story of nine-year-old Eller Juanita Tuten, who died following an accidental fire at her grandparents' Miami home in June 1958, and her beloved terrier Trixy, who died just hours later.
author: Family Archive Research

sections.heading: A Childhood in Miami
sections.text: Eller Juanita Tuten was born in 1948. She was the granddaughter of Eller Matthews Mathis and the step-granddaughter of Glover Mathis. Contemporary newspaper accounts identify her father as Thomas Tuten and her mother as Mrs. Juanita Tuten. Family research suggests that her parents were Thomas Loise Tuten and Juanita Wells, although their identities require further verification. Her parents were divorced, and Juanita had lived with her grandparents since birth at 8475 SW 4th Street in Miami, Florida. Juanita had cerebral palsy, a condition she had lived with since birth. According to her father, she attended school and participated in everyday activities. One of her closest companions was Trixy, a small terrier who had been part of her life for several years. Newspaper accounts described the two as inseparable.

sections.heading: The Accident
sections.text: On June 18, 1958, a tragic accident occurred at the Mathis family home in Miami. According to contemporary newspaper reports, Juanita had been playing with a cigarette lighter when she accidentally ignited a piece of paper. The flames spread to her clothing. When her grandparents discovered what had happened, they attempted to extinguish the flames and rushed her to Jackson Memorial Hospital. Juanita suffered extensive burns and remained hospitalized in critical condition. Her father, Thomas Tuten, later told reporters that he and his family had visited Juanita regularly and that she had received good care from her grandparents. He described the incident as a terrible accident.

sections.heading: Her Final Days
sections.text: During her hospitalization, Juanita repeatedly asked for Trixy. The little dog had been placed in the care of neighbors while Juanita was in the hospital. On June 26, 1958, Juanita died at Jackson Memorial Hospital in Miami. She was nine years old. According to a June 27 article in The Miami Herald, her final words were a call for her beloved dog. The newspaper account provides a glimpse of the close companionship that had existed between Juanita and Trixy throughout her childhood.

sections.heading: Together Even in Death
sections.text: Later that same morning, Trixy was struck and killed by an automobile. The deaths of Juanita and her beloved dog within hours of one another attracted widespread attention. Newspapers across Florida and beyond published accounts of the unusual and sorrowful coincidence. Juanita's uncle William Tuten described the two as constant companions. Juanita's funeral arrangements were handled by Ben Lanier & Son in Miami. She was buried at Woodlawn Park North Cemetery and Mausoleum in Miami, where her gravestone records the years 1948–1958. Trixy was buried behind the Mathis family home at 8475 SW 4th Street. According to newspaper reports, the family planned to place a small monument at the dog's resting place.

sections.heading: Remembering Juanita
sections.text: Although the newspaper coverage focused heavily on the circumstances of their deaths, the surviving accounts also preserve something of Juanita's life: a young girl who attended school, lived with her grandparents, and shared a close bond with a beloved companion. Her childhood photograph, gravestone, and the contemporary newspaper reports preserve her place in the Mathis-Matthews-Tuten family history. The historical address of her grandparents' Miami home provides another connection to the places where the family lived. Nearly seven decades later, the story of Juanita and Trixy remains a poignant chapter in the family's past.

sections.heading: Sources and Research Notes
sections.text: Contemporary newspaper coverage includes The Miami News, June 19, 1958; The Miami Herald, June 19 and June 27, 1958; the Tallahassee Democrat, June 28, 1958; and The Ledger, June 29, 1958. These accounts document Juanita's accident, hospitalization, death, family relationships, and the death of her dog Trixy. A newspaper article by Joseph Hoffman identifies her father as Thomas Tuten. Another identifies her mother as Mrs. Juanita Tuten. The identification of these individuals as Thomas Loise Tuten and Juanita Wells is based on family research and awaits additional documentation. Juanita's gravestone records 1948–1958, while her cemetery memorial identifies June 26, 1958, as her death date and Section 9A of Woodlawn Park North Cemetery as her burial location. Some newspaper reports differ in minor details, including the duration of Juanita's companionship with Trixy.
